Sample text:
---
### Things, Not People

My grandfather’s shop stood between a bakery and a locksmith, so all morning it smelled of bread and brass. Above the door he had painted REPAIRS. Underneath, in smaller letters: THINGS, NOT PEOPLE.

I came back in November to sell the lease. The shop had been closed for six weeks, but some of the clocks were still going, each keeping a slightly different afternoon. On the workbench lay his notebook. Instead of accounts, the first page contained four rules:

*Listen before you look.*  
*Never force a small screw.*  
*A rattle is not always a fault.*  
*Return what you cannot mend.*

I put the notebook in the box marked RUBBISH. Then I took it out again.

The bell rang, though I had turned the sign to CLOSED. A woman stood on the mat, rain bright on her green coat, holding a cassette tape in both hands.

“Are you open?”

“No.”

She looked at the clocks. “Which one of them decided that?”

I let her in. Her name was Ellen. The tape held forty-three seconds recorded in her mother’s kitchen in 1986: a song, dishes in a sink, a chair scraping back. Her mother had died when Ellen was nineteen.

“It used to play,” she said. “Now it only hisses.”

I opened the plastic shell. The ribbon was creased near the beginning, a brown pleat no wider than an eyelash. My hands remembered work my mind had forgotten: summer afternoons, the smell of solder, my grandfather saying, *Don’t pull. Coax.*

While I cleaned the ribbon, Ellen walked around the shop.

“He repaired my pram,” she said. “Before I was born. Charged my mother sixpence and a tomato.”

“That sounds like him.”

“She said he talked to it while he worked.”

“He talked to everything.”

“Did it help?”

“Usually he ran out of things to say and fixed it by accident.”

She laughed, then covered her mouth, though there was no one there to scold her.

When the tape was ready, she sat beside the counter.

“On the recording, I’m fifteen,” she said. “Mum asks me to sing with her, and I say, *Not now.* I remember thinking there would be another afternoon. I have no idea what I was so busy with.”

“What happens after?”

“That’s what I can’t remember. I’ve heard it hundreds of times, but I start listening so hard for what I want that I miss what she says.” She looked at the little brown reels. “Sometimes I think there must be another version. One where I put down whatever I was doing.”

I could have told her there wasn’t. Instead, I made tea. We drank it while the clocks disagreed.

At last I put the cassette into my grandfather’s player. The speaker gave a small cough.

Water ran into a sink. Crockery knocked together. A woman sang three lines of a song, cheerfully ignoring the difficult notes. Then, farther from the microphone, a girl said, “Not now, Mum.”

The singing stopped.

“All right,” the mother said. A drawer opened. “Later, then.”

The tape hissed. Beneath the hiss, she began humming again. After four notes, the recording ended.

Ellen didn’t move. I wanted to rewind it, but something in her face made me wait.

“She went on humming,” she said.

“Yes.”

“I thought she’d been hurt.”

“Perhaps she was.”

Ellen nodded. “Perhaps she was.”

I copied the tape and gave her both cassettes. When she asked what she owed, I looked at the rain polishing the window.

“Do you have a tomato?”

“No.”

“Then we’ll pretend you paid.”

After she left, I took the CLOSED sign out of the window. I was not ready for customers, but I retrieved the notebook and added a fifth rule:

*Do not mistake an ending for a verdict.*

It explained too much. My grandfather would have crossed it out.

Outside, the bakery pulled down its blind. The locksmith’s light went off. One by one, the clocks reached six, though it took them nearly a minute to agree.

Before going home, I turned the sign over and wrote:

OPEN TOMORROW.

Then, because tomorrow can be a promise or merely a direction, I added:

PROBABLY.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: VARY

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A quiet literary story uses a repair shop and a damaged recording to explore grief, regret, and the limits of what can be repaired.

## Grounded reading
The voice is patient and gently wry, letting small gestures carry emotional weight: taking the notebook back out of the rubbish, making tea, waiting before rewinding. Its pathos comes from the gap between what Ellen remembers and what the tape actually preserves—not a clean reconciliation, but a mother humming after a painful exchange. The story invites the reader to listen without forcing a verdict, and to accept that care can mean leaving some uncertainty intact.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds ordinary objects as carriers of memory: clocks keeping different time, a cassette tape, a repair notebook, a tomato. Repair becomes both a craft and a moral metaphor, but the story resists making it a cure for grief or regret. Its closing “PROBABLY” keeps hope present while refusing to turn tomorrow into a guarantee.

## Evidence line
> The shop had been closed for six weeks, but some of the clocks were still going, each keeping a slightly different afternoon.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The recurring repair imagery, careful emotional restraint, and qualified ending make this a distinctive, coherent sample with unusually deliberate choices.
